Optimizing Oxygenation and Hemodynamics

Improve gas exchange, protect the lungs and preserve circulation.

Complete each block to unlock the next. Optional practice is available for additional review.
Lesson competencies

Optimize oxygenation: beyond the saturation

You have already learned to assess ventilation and interpret ventilator graphics. Now connect gas exchange to circulation. A patient’s SpO₂ rises after PEEP is increased, but blood pressure falls. Has the intervention actually helped?

Before PEEP adjustmentSpO₂ 88%BP 118/72 mmHgPEEP 8 cmH₂O
After PEEP adjustmentSpO₂ 96%BP 82/46 mmHgPEEP 14 cmH₂O

Both readings are confirmed in this teaching scenario. The patient has bilateral pneumonia. The fall in blood pressure requires immediate assessment and coordinated intervention; do not wait for another ABG. Later, we will use mechanics and circulation data to decide whether the PEEP change was beneficial.

Instructor explainer · MV-2.3-V00 · recording pending

A better saturation. A worse patient?

▶Instructor video placeholderRecording to be added before publication
Draft transcript

You increase PEEP for a patient with pneumonia. Saturation rises from 88 to 96 percent. But look at the blood pressure: 118 over 72 becomes 82 over 46. Is the patient really better? Oxygen must reach the alveoli, transfer into blood, bind to hemoglobin, and travel to tissues. A ventilator can improve the first two steps while pressure changes impair circulation. In 2.1 you learned to interpret blood gases and mechanics. In 2.2 you learned to read the breath. Now we will use those tools to find the cause of hypoxemia, select support, and check the cardiovascular response. A falling pressure needs immediate attention, not another routine blood gas. Our challenge is to improve gas exchange without sacrificing lung protection or oxygen delivery.

III.C.3.a · Invasive ventilator settingsIII.E.2.o · Ventilation recommendations

NBRC RTE 2027 detailed content outline

1 · DifferentiateOxygen pressure, saturation, content and delivery.
2 · InterpretMechanisms of hypoxemia and ABG findings.
3 · CalculateP/F, PAO₂, A–aO₂, CaO₂, CvO₂, DO₂ and shunt fraction.
4 · RecommendCombined ventilation and oxygenation adjustments within protective limits.
5 · EvaluateReassess the patient’s response rather than one number.
Bring the reasoning forward: assess gas exchange → identify the mechanism → choose targeted support → reassess oxygenation, mechanics and circulation.

This portion establishes the assessment skills used later in PEEP titration and hemodynamic monitoring.

1 · Oxygen transport

Four different oxygen measurements

Imagine a patient with severe anemia. The monitor shows 98% saturation. The ABG shows a normal PaO₂. Yet the patient is tachycardic and has signs of inadequate perfusion. The monitor is not necessarily wrong: it is answering only one of our questions.

01 · Into the lungAlveolar oxygen

FiO₂ and alveolar ventilation determine oxygen available for exchange.

02 · Into the bloodGas exchange

PaO₂ reflects dissolved oxygen pressure after transfer into arterial blood.

03 · Carry oxygenHemoglobin + plasma

SaO₂ describes occupied binding sites. CaO₂ counts oxygen carried per dL.

04 · Deliver oxygenCardiac output

DO₂ combines oxygen content and blood flow to systemic tissues.

MeasurementWhat it tells youWhat it cannot tell you alone
PaO₂Pressure exerted by dissolved oxygen in arterial bloodTotal oxygen carried
SaO₂ / SpO₂Fraction of hemoglobin binding sites occupied; SpO₂ is a pulse oximeter estimateHemoglobin concentration or blood flow
CaO₂Oxygen carried per dL of arterial bloodHow much reaches tissues per minute
DO₂Oxygen delivered to systemic circulation per minuteWhether individual tissues receive or extract enough
Think of oxygen transport as a bus service. Hemoglobin is the number of seats; saturation is the proportion occupied; cardiac output is the amount of blood moving per minute. A nearly full bus can still carry too few passengers.
Instructor explainer · MV-2.3-V01 · recording pending

Where is the oxygen going?

▶Instructor video placeholderRecording to be added before publication
Draft transcript

Two patients have a saturation of 98 percent. One has a normal hemoglobin concentration; the other has severe anemia. Saturation tells us the proportion of binding sites occupied, not how many sites exist. Think of two buses, one with many seats and one with very few. Both can be almost full, yet one carries far fewer passengers. Most oxygen travels bound to hemoglobin, with a small amount dissolved in plasma. PaO₂ describes the pressure of dissolved oxygen. CaO₂ tells us the total amount carried in each deciliter. Now add cardiac output: even blood with normal content cannot deliver enough oxygen if too little blood is circulating. In the explorer, change hemoglobin without changing PaO₂, then change cardiac output. Which measurement changes, and which stays the same?

HypoxemiaLow arterial oxygenation.
HypoxiaInadequate oxygen availability or utilization at tissue level.
HyperoxiaExcess oxygen exposure; more is not always better.

Pulse oximetry is affected by poor perfusion, movement, dyshemoglobins and device limitations including skin pigmentation-related error. Confirm unexpected readings with appropriate assessment and arterial sampling. Oxygen targets depend on the disease, risk of hypercapnia and clinical protocol.

1 · Interactive physiology

Explore oxygen content and delivery

Adjust hemoglobin, arterial oxygenation and cardiac output. Notice which variable changes content and which changes delivery without changing content.

CaO₂ = (1.34 × Hb × SaO₂) + (0.003 × PaO₂)
DO₂ = CaO₂ × CO × 10

Use saturation as a decimal. CaO₂ is mL O₂/dL; cardiac output is L/min; 10 converts liters to deciliters.

WORKED EXAMPLE 1

Calculate arterial oxygen content

Hemoglobin15 g/dL
Measured SaO₂98%
PaO₂95 mmHg
1
Convert saturation to a decimal.
98 ÷ 100 = 0.98
2
Calculate hemoglobin-bound oxygen.
1.34 × 15 × 0.98 = 19.698 mL/dL
3
Calculate dissolved oxygen.
0.003 × 95 = 0.285 mL/dL
Add the two componentsCaO₂ = 19.98 mL O₂/dL

Almost all the oxygen is carried by hemoglobin. Keep unrounded values for the next calculation.

WORKED EXAMPLE 2

Calculate systemic oxygen delivery

CaO₂ from example 119.983 mL/dL
Cardiac output5 L/min
1
Convert blood flow to dL/min.
5 L/min × 10 dL/L = 50 dL/min
2
Multiply content by flow.
19.983 × 50 = 999.15 mL O₂/min
Rounded to a whole numberDO₂ = 999 mL O₂/min

If cardiac output falls by half while content is unchanged, delivery also falls by half. Delivery is not a direct measurement of tissue oxygen utilization.

Predict, change, observe

First predict what happens to content and delivery if hemoglobin falls but PaO₂ stays unchanged. Then test the prediction. Next, reduce cardiac output alone. Finally, vary PaO₂ and watch the saturation curve.

Estimated SaO₂
CaO₂ (mL/dL)
DO₂ (mL/min)
What makes up CaO₂?

Hb-bound: mL/dL   Dissolved: mL/dL

Common scale: 0–26 mL/dL

Illustrative Hill curve, P50 26.6 mmHg, normal affinity assumed. Acidosis, temperature and other factors shift the actual curve. Use measured saturation for clinical calculations.

At higher PaO₂ the curve flattens: increases in PaO₂ contribute relatively little to hemoglobin-bound oxygen once hemoglobin is nearly saturated. On the steep portion, a small fall in PaO₂ may substantially decrease saturation. A right shift facilitates unloading but reduces saturation at a given PaO₂; a left shift does the opposite.

Apply what you observed

PaO₂ and SaO₂ remain unchanged after cardiac output falls from 5 to 2.5 L/min. Hemoglobin is unchanged. Which response is expected?

2 · Mechanisms of hypoxemia

Why is oxygen not reaching arterial blood?

Before recommending PEEP or FiO₂, ask what is preventing oxygen transfer. Five mechanisms explain most arterial hypoxemia. More than one may be present.

MechanismClinical clueExpected oxygen response
Low inspired oxygenGas supply or altitudeUsually improves with adequate inspired oxygen
Alveolar hypoventilationElevated PaCO₂; A–a gradient may be normalOxygen helps PaO₂; ventilation still needs correction
Diffusion limitationThickened alveolar-capillary barrierUsually improves
Low V/QPerfusion exceeds regional ventilationOften improves
Right-to-left shuntBlood bypasses ventilated units, e.g. consolidated or collapsed alveoliLimited response when shunt is large
Matched unit

Air meets blood; gas exchange occurs.

Shunt

Blood passes without ventilation.

Dead space

Air reaches an unperfused unit.

Dead space primarily wastes ventilation. A pulmonary embolism may also cause hypoxemia through redistribution of perfusion and associated V/Q mismatch. A collapsed but recruitable alveolus may respond to PEEP; consolidated or nonrecruitable tissue may not.

Follow the oxygen pathway to identify the problem

Begin with what is reaching the alveoli. If inspired oxygen is low or alveolar ventilation is inadequate, alveolar oxygen pressure falls. If enough oxygen is available in the alveoli but arterial oxygen remains low, investigate gas exchange across the lung.

Patient with sedative-related hypoventilationOn room air at sea level: PaCO₂ 60, PaO₂ 68. With the simplified alveolar gas equation, PAO₂ is about 75 mmHg and the A–a gradient is about 7 mmHg. Oxygen transfer is relatively preserved; effective alveolar ventilation is the problem. Supplemental oxygen can improve PaO₂ without correcting CO₂ retention.
Patient with pulmonary edemaOn room air at sea level: PaCO₂ 40, PaO₂ 55. Estimated PAO₂ is about 100 mmHg and the A–a gradient is about 45 mmHg. Oxygen is available but transfer is impaired. Partly ventilated, perfused regions may improve with oxygen; completely unventilated perfused regions may respond poorly.

Clinical connection: A large A–a gradient identifies impaired transfer, not its exact cause. Combine the ABG with clinical findings, imaging, mechanics and oxygen response. Do not infer recruitability from the gradient alone.

The next activity asks you to distinguish mechanisms; the following section shows exactly how to calculate the pressures used here.

3 · Applied calculations

Quantify oxygenation: P/F and A–a gradient

Bring forward the formulas from last semester. The P/F ratio describes arterial oxygenation relative to the oxygen provided. The A–a gradient compares estimated alveolar oxygen with measured arterial oxygen.

P/F = PaO₂ ÷ FiO₂
PAO₂ ≈ FiO₂ × (PB − 47) − PaCO₂ / 0.8
A–aO₂ = PAO₂ − PaO₂

Use FiO₂ as a decimal, PB in mmHg, water vapor pressure 47 mmHg at body temperature, and an assumed respiratory quotient of 0.8. This is the simplified alveolar gas equation; its approximation becomes less accurate at high FiO₂. Use the stated convention consistently in these exercises.

WORKED EXAMPLE · BILATERAL PNEUMONIA

How much oxygen reaches the arterial blood?

FiO₂0.50
PaO₂52 mmHg
PaCO₂60 mmHg
PB760 mmHg
1
Relate arterial oxygen to the support provided.
P/F = 52 / 0.50 = 104 mmHg
Use the fraction, not 50. A low ratio indicates substantial impairment relative to the oxygen supplied.
2
Estimate alveolar oxygen pressure.
PB − 47 = 713 mmHg
PAO₂ = (0.50 × 713) − (60 / 0.8)
= 356.5 − 75 = 281.5 mmHg
Water vapor reduces the available inspired gas pressure; alveolar CO₂ further reduces estimated alveolar oxygen.
3
Compare alveolar with arterial oxygen.
A–a = 281.5 − 52 = 229.5 mmHg
Subtract measured arterial oxygen from estimated alveolar oxygen, not the reverse.
Interpret the pattern

Both the elevated PaCO₂ and the large A–a gradient need attention. Improving ventilation alone is unlikely to resolve the oxygen transfer impairment. P/F alone does not diagnose ARDS.

A–a gradient depends on age, FiO₂ and barometric pressure. Trend P/F in context of PEEP, FiO₂ and timing; do not treat the ratio as independent of ventilator support.

Which measurement answers which question? P/F compares oxygenation to support; PAO₂ estimates oxygen available in the alveolus; A–a estimates the pressure difference across the gas exchange pathway. None measures oxygen content or delivery. A normal PaO₂ on substantial FiO₂ does not establish normal gas exchange. In practice compare trends under documented support and use age, altitude and FiO₂ context when interpreting A–a.

3 · Shunt fraction

Where does shunted blood go?

Blood leaving ventilated alveoli mixes with blood that did not fully participate in gas exchange. The physiological shunt equation estimates the fraction of cardiac output behaving as shunted blood under the measurement conditions.

Qs/Qt (%) = 100 × (CcO₂ − CaO₂) / (CcO₂ − CvO₂)
CcO₂Ideal end-capillary content: 1.34 × Hb × 1.0 + .003 × PAO₂.
CaO₂Measured arterial content: 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + .003 × PaO₂.
CvO₂Mixed venous content: 1.34 × Hb × SvO₂ + .003 × PvO₂.

Mixed venous blood is sampled from the pulmonary artery when a PA catheter is clinically indicated. Central venous saturation is not interchangeable with mixed venous saturation. At less than 100% inspired oxygen, the calculated physiological shunt can include effects of low V/Q; it is not a pure anatomical shunt measurement.

WORKED EXAMPLE · VENOUS ADMIXTURE

Trace the oxygen content through the lung

MeasurementValueMeasurementValue
Hb12 g/dLFiO₂0.50
PB760 mmHgPaCO₂40 mmHg
PaO₂ / SaO₂60 mmHg / 90%PvO₂ / SvO₂40 mmHg / 75%
1
Estimate PAO₂ before calculating ideal end-capillary content.
PAO₂ = 0.50 × (760 − 47) − 40/0.8 = 306.5 mmHg
2
Calculate the content of blood leaving an ideal ventilated unit.
CcO₂ = (1.34 × 12 × 1.00) + (0.003 × 306.5)
= 16.9995 mL/dL
For this exercise assume ideal end-capillary saturation is 100% at this PAO₂. Use alveolar pressure as the ideal end-capillary PO₂.
3
Calculate the content of mixed arterial blood.
CaO₂ = (1.34 × 12 × 0.90) + (0.003 × 60)
= 14.652 mL/dL
Use measured arterial saturation and pressure.
4
Calculate the content of incoming mixed venous blood.
CvO₂ = (1.34 × 12 × 0.75) + (0.003 × 40)
= 12.18 mL/dL
Use mixed venous data, not arterial or central venous substitutes.
5
Compare the loss of oxygen content with the maximum possible gain.
Qs/Qt = 100 × (16.9995 − 14.652) / (16.9995 − 12.18)
= 48.7%
What does this mean?

A large estimated physiological shunt suggests substantial venous admixture. At this FiO₂, low V/Q can contribute. It does not establish that the lung is recruitable. Keep intermediate precision; round the final percent to one decimal.

3 · Combined management

Read the entire ABG before changing settings

First identify the acid–base disturbance and whether compensation is appropriate. Then judge oxygenation in relation to FiO₂ and support. A patient can require changes to both ventilation and oxygenation, or to neither.

ABG patternVentilation decisionOxygenation decision
Respiratory acidosis + hypoxemiaIncrease effective ventilation if safeImprove oxygenation
Respiratory alkalosis + hypoxemiaReduce excessive support if appropriate; evaluate driveImprove oxygenation
Metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensationPreserve compensatory ventilationTitrate oxygen to target
Adequate gas exchange on excessive supportEvaluate reduction in supportReduce unnecessary FiO₂
Desired VE ≈ current VE × current PaCO₂ / target PaCO₂
Expected PaCO₂ in metabolic acidosis = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2

The VE estimate assumes unchanged CO₂ production and dead-space fraction. Use an appropriate PaCO₂/pH target, not automatically 40. In VC, preserve protective VT where possible and evaluate expiratory time when increasing rate. In PC, changes in pressure can change delivered VT. Avoid suppressing necessary compensatory ventilation.

Worked decision · Two problems, two goals

A different patient on passive VC-A/C has PBW 60 kg, VT 360 mL, RR 15, FiO₂ 0.45, PEEP 8. ABG: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 55, PaO₂ 59, HCO₃⁻ 26. Stable circulation, plateau 24 and complete exhalation. For this exercise the team targets PaCO₂ 40 and SpO₂ 92–96%.

1
Identify the disturbance. Acidemia with elevated PaCO₂ and a modest bicarbonate rise is consistent with acute respiratory acidosis. Oxygenation is also inadequate relative to support.
2
Estimate ventilation needed.
Current VE = 0.360 × 15 = 5.4 L/min
Desired VE = 5.4 × 55/40 ≈ 7.4 L/min
Estimated RR = 15 × 55/40 ≈ 21/min
Keep VT at 6 mL/kg PBW. Check pressure, expiratory time, total rate and tolerance before accepting the estimate.
3
Address oxygenation separately. Titrate FiO₂ to the prescribed target; consider a monitored PEEP trial if impaired recruitment is suspected. Do not assume the PaO₂ will rise proportionally to FiO₂. In a stable patient, make targeted changes one at a time when feasible. Significant hypoxemia or instability requires prompt support, not waiting for a routine ABG.
4
Reassess both goals. Compare repeat pH, PaCO₂, oxygenation, pressures, expiratory flow and BP with baseline. Maintain settings that meet goals safely; reduce unnecessary support when appropriate.
Metabolic acidosis is different. Example: HCO₃⁻ 16, PaCO₂ 32. Winter’s formula gives 1.5 × 16 + 8 = 32 mmHg, with an expected range of 30–34. The low PaCO₂ is appropriate compensation, not a reason to reduce ventilation. Address the metabolic cause and any separate oxygenation deficit.

4 · FiO₂

More oxygen: the first lever, not the only lever

Return to the patient with pneumonia. The airway is patent, the circuit is intact and the team has assessed the patient. FiO₂ is .50 and PaO₂ is 52 mmHg. Increasing FiO₂ raises inspired oxygen pressure immediately; it does not reopen an obstructed or collapsed alveolus.

Immediate rescueWhen oxygenation is dangerously low, promptly increase oxygen support while addressing the cause. Brief use of FiO₂ 1.0 may be appropriate in emergencies.
Once stabilizedTitrate toward the ordered target; unnecessary exposure to high oxygen concentrations contributes to oxidative injury and absorption atelectasis.

The AARC acute-care guideline suggests SpO₂ 94–98% for most hospitalized adults and 88–92% for adults with COPD receiving oxygen. ARDS protocols may intentionally use lower targets (e.g., SpO₂ 88–95%). Individualize for the clinical condition and prescribed target; do not apply one target to every patient.

Absorption atelectasis: Nitrogen helps maintain alveolar gas volume. When high FiO₂ replaces nitrogen in poorly ventilated units, oxygen can be absorbed faster than gas is replenished, promoting collapse. High oxygen exposure and duration both matter; there is no universal safe cutoff.

Compare the two illustrative patients below. Both begin with PaO₂ 52; their response to oxygen differs because their gas exchange mechanisms differ.

Low V/Q predominant
Large shunt predominant

Illustrative responses, not a predictive model or treatment protocol. Both patients require reassessment.

When a large shunt limits the effect of FiO₂, consider whether lung units are recruitable, whether secretions or positioning are contributing, and whether treating the underlying cause can improve gas exchange.

AARC oxygen guideline (2022)

5 · PEEP physiology

Open the lung, keep it open

At the end of expiration, alveoli are at risk of collapse when their distending pressure is insufficient. Surfactant reduces surface tension and stabilizes smaller alveoli; edema, inflammation and loss of surfactant make collapse more likely. PEEP raises end-expiratory airway pressure, often increasing end-expiratory lung volume (EELV). Functional residual capacity describes resting lung volume at the end of a passive breath without applied pressure.

Opening pressurePressure needed to reopen a closed unit may be greater than the pressure required to keep it open.
Closing pressureBelow this pressure a vulnerable unit may collapse again. PEEP can help prevent repeated closing.

Explore a heterogeneous lung

Move the PEEP slider to select each of the four pressure levels. Start at 5 cmH₂O and increase gradually. Watch which clusters recruit, which stretch excessively and how the surrounding capillary changes. Compare the open and overdistended counts before deciding where recruitment is balanced against distension.

Open units
Overdistended units
Model response

Conceptual illustration only. Real opening/closing pressures differ among units, and PEEP does not predict recruitability by itself.

Apply what you observed

At the highest modeled PEEP, some capillaries narrow even though more lung units are open. What does this suggest?

Recruitment can reduce shunt and improve compliance; overdistension can compress capillaries, increase dead space, reduce compliance and impair right ventricular function. Both can occur simultaneously in different lung regions.

PEEP is not a recruitment maneuver. Sustaining end-expiratory pressure differs from deliberately applying high pressure to reopen units. The 2024 ATS ARDS guideline conditionally favors higher PEEP without recruitment maneuvers in moderate-to-severe ARDS and recommends against prolonged recruitment maneuvers. Detailed ARDS protocols follow in advanced management.

ATS ARDS guideline update (2024)

5 · Mechanics

Recruitment or overdistension?

Think back to the pressure–volume loops in 2.2. The lower portion of a slow pressure–volume curve may reflect opening of lung units; the flattening upper portion may reflect decreasing compliance. A bird’s beak on a dynamic loop is a warning of possible overdistension, not a standalone prescription for PEEP. Inflection points are not precise individual opening or closing pressures, and dynamic loops are affected by resistance and effort.

At constant VT under passive conditions, with valid holds and no leak, compare driving pressure and static compliance at each PEEP:

ΔP = Pplat − total PEEP
Cstat = VT / ΔP
PEEPPlateauΔPCstat (VT 400)
5292416.7
10281822.2
15362119.0

All pressures are cmH₂O; total PEEP equals set PEEP in this example. At 10, compliance improves and driving pressure falls, consistent with recruitment. At 15, plateau rises and compliance falls, suggesting excessive distension. Neither observation alone proves the regional mechanism. Check oxygenation, circulation, effort and measurement quality.

Reducing VT while maintaining adequate PEEP can limit end-inspiratory stress without sacrificing end-expiratory stability. The two adjustments address different parts of the breath.

6 · Mean airway pressure

Pressure over time, not just peak pressure

Mean airway pressure (Paw) is the time average of airway pressure across the entire respiratory cycle. A brief high peak contributes less area than a sustained pressure. Increasing mean airway pressure may improve oxygenation by supporting lung volume, but it is not a direct measure of alveolar recruitment or pleural pressure.

Ideal square-pressure breath: mean Paw = PEEP + ΔPinsp × Ti / Ttotal
Ttotal = 60 / RR; Te = Ttotal − Ti

For PC at PEEP 5, pressure above PEEP 15, RR 20 and Ti 1 s: mean Paw = 5 + 15 × 1/3 = 10 cmH₂O. If Ti becomes 1.5 s, mean Paw increases to 12.5, but Te falls from 2 to 1.5 s.

Pressure–time laboratory

Mean Paw
Peak pressure
Expiratory time

Idealized PC square pressure with fixed pressure 15 cmH₂O above PEEP, no rise time, no intrinsic PEEP. Ti is limited to leave at least 0.2 s of expiration; this limit is not a clinical safety threshold.

AdjustmentExpected mean Paw effectTradeoff
Increase PEEPIncreases, other pressures relative to PEEP held constantHemodynamics, recruitment vs distension
Increase TiUsually increases at fixed pressureShorter Te; possible trapping
Increase PC pressureIncreasesVT and distending pressure may rise
Increase RRMay increase if Ti unchangedShorter Te
Change VC flowVariable; changes pressure and timingPeak pressure and synchrony

In real VC and PC, waveform shape, rise time, spontaneous effort and intrinsic PEEP influence measured mean Paw. Do not apply the square-pressure formula to every mode.

7 · Heart–lung interactions

Why does blood pressure fall when PEEP rises?

You have increased PEEP for a patient with pneumonia. The saturation rises, but arterial pressure begins to fall. The airway is patent and the patient has been assessed. To understand the response, follow the blood back to the heart.

During spontaneous inspiration, pleural pressure normally falls, helping lower right atrial pressure relative to the systemic circulation. During passive positive-pressure inspiration, airway pressure rises and some of that pressure is transmitted to the pleural space. During expiration, pressure decreases. Applied PEEP raises the end-expiratory airway pressure and may keep pleural pressure elevated between breaths, reducing the opportunity for venous return to recover.

Conceptual pressure traces, not actual patient waveforms or measured airway pressure. Transmission of airway pressure to pleural pressure varies with lung/chest-wall mechanics and effort.

Memory hook: PEEP changes the baseline, not just the peak. The circulation experiences the pressure throughout the breath cycle.
7 · Venous return

Blood moves down a pressure gradient

Think of the systemic veins as the reservoir feeding the right atrium. Mean systemic filling pressure (Pms) represents the upstream pressure available to drive venous return. Right atrial pressure (PRA) is the downstream pressure. Resistance to venous return opposes flow.

Venous return = (Pms − PRA) / RVR

If Pms remains 10 mmHg and PRA increases from 2 to 7 mmHg, the driving pressure decreases from 8 to 3 mmHg. At unchanged resistance, venous return falls. In a real patient Pms and resistance may also change; this is a model, not a PEEP-to-CVP conversion.

Venous return laboratory

Driving pressure
Illustrative forward flow

Resistance fixed at 2 mmHg/(L/min); forward flow clipped at zero. This model does not predict actual cardiac output.

Reduced RV filling can reduce RV stroke volume, then LV filling and systemic cardiac output. Blood pressure may fall if vascular compensation is insufficient. A patient with low circulating volume may be particularly vulnerable.

7 · Ventricular loading

A higher CVP does not guarantee better filling

Measured CVP approximates right atrial pressure relative to atmosphere. The pressure distending the atrium is the difference between pressure inside and pressure surrounding it. When surrounding pressure rises, measured CVP may rise while effective filling pressure falls.

Illustrative transmural pressure = intracardiac pressure − surrounding pressure
Measurement (mmHg)BeforeAfter
Measured RA pressure410
Surrounding pressure08
Transmural pressure42

Do not subtract set PEEP from CVP: airway pressure and surrounding cardiac pressure are different quantities, with different units and variable transmission.

Right ventricleVery high lung volumes may compress alveolar vessels and increase pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), raising RV afterload. Recruitment from low lung volume can instead reduce PVR. A struggling RV can dilate and interfere with LV filling.
Left ventriclePositive intrathoracic pressure can lower LV transmural systolic pressure and reduce LV afterload. In selected patients with cardiogenic pulmonary edema this may improve cardiac performance. Reduced preload can still be harmful in other patients.
PEEP is not inherently harmful or beneficial to circulation. The response depends on volume status, lung volume, ventricular function and pressure transmission.

7 · Monitoring

Which monitor answers the clinical question?

When support increases, choose monitoring based on the information needed. Pulse oximetry trends saturation; capnography trends exhaled CO₂ and waveform integrity. Neither replaces ABG measurement when precise arterial gas exchange and pH are needed.

DeviceWhat it measuresWhen useful
BP cuffIntermittent BP/MAP estimateStable circulation; corroborating invasive readings
Arterial catheterDirect continuous arterial pressure; arterial blood samplingLabile BP, vasoactive titration, repeated ABGs
Central venous catheterCVP; central venous blood sampling (ScvO₂)Selected assessment and vascular access
Pulmonary artery catheter (PAC)RA/CVP, PAP, PAOP, CO, mixed venous saturation (SvO₂)Selected complex shock or cardiopulmonary assessment
EchocardiographyCardiac structure, RV/LV function, estimated flowInvestigate circulatory compromise

ScvO₂ from a central venous catheter samples primarily upper-body return and is not interchangeable with true mixed venous SvO₂ sampled from the pulmonary artery. Use the appropriate mixed venous sample for physiological shunt calculations.

RT responsibilities vary by facility; understand the measurements even when another clinician manages the catheter.

7 · Arterial monitoring

From artery to bedside monitor

An arterial catheter is commonly placed in the radial artery; femoral and other sites may be appropriate. A fluid-filled pressure system transmits the arterial pulse to a transducer, which converts pressure into an electrical signal. A pressurized flush system maintains patency according to local policy. The line permits repeated arterial sampling without repeated punctures.

Continuous BP is valuable during PEEP trials and vasopressor titration because a cuff reading may miss rapid changes. However, an invasive reading is only as reliable as its reference level and system response.

Level to the intended reference (typically right atrial level at the fourth intercostal space, midaxillary line for systemic BP), zero to atmosphere according to protocol, and verify waveform quality. Relevel after repositioning. A transducer above the reference reads falsely low; below reads falsely high.

Explore transducer height

True BP120/72
Displayed BP
Displayed MAP

Idealized hydrostatic error of about 0.75 mmHg per cm of vertical difference; other errors excluded.

Complications include bleeding, infection, thrombosis, distal ischemia and sampling-related blood loss. Inspect the site and distal perfusion; do not force a flush against suspected obstruction. Detailed waveform and equipment troubleshooting follows in 2.4.

7 · Hemodynamic interpretation

Follow the pressure through the circulation

Pressures are measured at specific points along the circulation. A PAC advances from a central vein through RA, RV and into the pulmonary artery. A brief balloon occlusion permits measurement of pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP, also called PAWP or PCWP) under appropriate conditions. PAOP estimates left atrial pressure, but PEEP, lung zones and cardiac disease may distort the relationship.

*PAOP is an indirect estimate of LA pressure, not a direct LA measurement.

VariableTypical adult referenceInterpretation
CVP2–6 mmHgRA pressure estimate, not volume status alone
PAP15–30 / 4–12 mmHgPulmonary vascular and cardiac loading
PAOP6–12 mmHgEstimate of LA pressure with valid measurement
CO4–8 L/minSystemic blood flow
CI2.5–4 L/min/m²CO indexed to body surface area
SvO₂60–80%Balance of delivery and consumption
MAP~70–100 mmHgArterial perfusion pressure; target individualized
MAP ≈ (SBP + 2 × DBP)/3
CI = CO/BSA
SV = CO × 1000/HR

Higher PAOP with pulmonary edema supports a hydrostatic component; low or normal PAOP may support permeability edema. Neither value alone diagnoses ARDS or cardiogenic edema. Elevated PAP can occur with embolism, hypoxic vasoconstriction or left heart disease; it is not diagnostic of PE. Focus on interpretation rather than catheter insertion.

8 · PEEP titration

Find the last effective and tolerated setting

A PEEP trial is a sequence of measured responses, not a contest to achieve the highest PaO₂. Use matched conditions when interpreting changes: stable VT, FiO₂, valid passive holds, adequate time for assessment and reliable BP. Establish patient-specific oxygenation and perfusion targets with the team.

Oxygenation and mechanicsPaO₂, SpO₂, P/F, plateau, total PEEP, driving pressure, compliance and expiratory flow.
Circulation and deliveryBP/MAP, HR, perfusion signs, CO and SvO₂ when available, and calculated DO₂ if data support it.

Here a passive VC patient (PBW 70 kg, VT 420 mL, FiO₂ .60, Hb 10 g/dL) has total PEEP equal to set PEEP. The airway and monitoring system have been assessed. The team is targeting PaO₂ at least 65 mmHg and MAP at least 65 mmHg for this example.

At 15, the incremental oxygenation benefit is small while MAP falls below the agreed target, CO falls and driving pressure rises. In this scenario, promptly return to 12 (the last tolerated effective step), evaluate other causes of hypotension, maintain oxygenation and reassess. Later, 10 might be sufficient too; the immediate question is which step to return to after the adverse response.

9 · Beyond ventilator settings

Treat the reason oxygen cannot reach blood

When the airway is patent and the ventilator functions correctly, ask whether changing a setting is the best way to improve gas exchange. A mucus plug, alveolar edema, consolidation and vascular obstruction produce different problems. Increasing oxygen can buy time without resolving the cause.

Restore ventilation to perfused regionsPositioning, indicated suctioning, bronchodilation for bronchospasm, and treatment of atelectasis can improve regional ventilation.
Treat the underlying diseaseAntimicrobial treatment for infection, appropriate management of pulmonary edema or embolism, and circulatory support address causes that ventilator adjustments alone cannot fix.

In unilateral disease, placing the better ventilated lung dependent may improve matching in selected patients; response is variable and clinical exceptions exist. Reassess oxygenation, mechanics and blood pressure rather than assuming a position always helps.

When secretions are evident, suction as indicated; preoxygenate and reassess. Avoid routine saline instillation. A transient oxygenation change after suction does not justify a permanent increase in ventilator support.

Source: AARC artificial airway suctioning guideline (2022). Equipment procedures and troubleshooting are covered in 2.4.

9 · Positioning and escalation

When protective ventilation alone is not enough

In supine ARDS, dependent dorsal regions may be compressed by the weight of the edematous lung and surrounding structures, while perfusion remains substantial there. Prone positioning can redistribute compression, make ventilation more homogeneous and improve ventilation–perfusion matching. It may also reduce regional stress even if the oxygen response is modest.

Conceptual regional aeration, not a quantitative prediction; perfusion and recruitability vary.

In severe ARDS, prolonged prone positioning (more than 12 hours per day) is recommended alongside lung-protective ventilation. Use trained staff and a protocol to protect the airway, lines, skin and hemodynamics. Selected patients may need neuromuscular blockade or consultation for VV-ECMO; inhaled pulmonary vasodilators may provide temporary oxygenation benefit in selected rescue situations but are not routine mortality-improving therapy.

Explore the effect of prone positioning

This simulated patient has severe oxygenation impairment. Select Prone patient, then compare the later reassessment with the baseline. FiO₂ and PEEP remain unchanged.

Supine · baseline assessment

SpO₂87%
PaO₂55 mmHg
P/F ratio92
FiO₂60%
PEEP12 cmH₂O
Arterial MAP78 mmHg

Observe the oxygenation impairment despite current ventilator support.

Illustrative scenario, not a predictive model or a device operation guide. Changes represent a later reassessment, not an instantaneous effect. Proning requires a trained team and protocol.

Why might oxygenation improve without changing ventilator settings?

Prone positioning can redistribute regional compression, improve ventilation homogeneity and improve matching of ventilation to perfusion. Response varies, and lack of an immediate oxygenation improvement does not establish lack of benefit.

Two ways to achieve prone positioning

Manual proning: A trained team turns and supports the patient on a conventional ICU bed, protecting the airway, lines and pressure points. Specialized rotational bed: A purpose-built system supports controlled repositioning according to its device-specific protocol. A rotational bed is not required for the physiological benefits of prone positioning.

Illustrations inspired by reference photographs; equipment details are not manufacturer instructions.

Do not substitute progressively injurious VT or pressure for escalation. Persistent severe hypoxemia despite optimized safe support warrants prompt team review.

Source: ATS ARDS guideline update (2024). Detailed advanced management follows in Unit 3.

10 · Clinical synthesis

One patient, two gas exchange problems

Now work through a patient without being told which setting needs adjustment. Start with pH and compensation; identify oxygenation impairment; then calculate the ventilation change and evaluate whether mechanics and circulation can tolerate it.

1 · InterpretABG, clinical target, P/F and A–aO₂.
2 · InterveneChoose the smallest reasonable changes that address the problems within protective limits.
3 · VerifyCheck measured VT, total rate, flow, plateau, total PEEP, BP and repeat gas exchange.

For constant VT and stable CO₂ production and dead-space fraction, estimate RR from current RR × current PaCO₂ / target PaCO₂. It is a starting estimate, not a guaranteed response. When both oxygenation and ventilation are unsafe, address both while monitoring for adverse effects; when stable, staged changes may help isolate the response.

10 · Final challenge

The limit of a ventilator adjustment

The most difficult decision may be to stop escalating a ventilator setting. If hypoxemia persists while plateau pressure, intrinsic PEEP or perfusion become unsafe, the next step may be an alternative strategy rather than a larger number.

A successful recommendation includes a goal, a safe setting or strategy, and an explicit reassessment plan. State what finding would make you reverse the intervention.

In the final case, use the provided clinical targets. Do not assume normal PaCO₂ is required or that more PEEP is automatically beneficial.

Lesson review

Essential notes and clinical pearls

Remember: oxygen pressure, saturation, content and delivery describe different steps of oxygen transport. P/F and A–a gradient quantify oxygenation impairment; neither replaces a patient assessment. Shunt calculations require appropriate mixed venous measurements. Interpret pH and compensation before selecting ventilation changes.

PEEP may narrow the venous return gradient. Restore the last tolerated effective PEEP when a trial causes significant hypotension, and reassess. Verify invasive pressure reference and waveform before interpreting data.

Frequently asked questions

Why not increase FiO₂ whenever DO₂ is low?

Once hemoglobin is nearly saturated, extra dissolved oxygen usually adds little content. Low hemoglobin or cardiac output may be the dominant problem.

Why can PaO₂ improve while DO₂ falls?

Cardiac output may fall enough to outweigh an improvement in CaO₂. This is why PEEP titration must include perfusion assessment.

Why not normalize all ABG values?

Compensation, chronic hypercapnia, lung protection and safe timing can make a different target appropriate.

Final clinical takeaways

Evaluate positioning and reversible causes when oxygenation remains inadequate. Preserve protective VT and patient-specific pH targets. Escalate when conventional support cannot meet gas exchange goals safely.

When should we stop increasing PEEP?

When additional PEEP produces important hemodynamic compromise, worsening mechanics or no meaningful benefit, reassess and return to a previously tolerated setting when appropriate.

Does every low P/F ratio mean ARDS?

No. Apply the full diagnostic criteria and clinical context; P/F alone measures oxygenation impairment.
